title: Purge expired sessions in place
blurb: Mutating a list inside a `for` loop is a famous trap — does this skip back-to-back expired sessions?
prompt: Spec: remove every session dict in `sessions` with `expires_at <= now` in place, and return how many active sessions remain. Tap a buggy line, or call it clean.
conclusion: AI summary: Drops all expired sessions in place (even consecutive ones) and returns the remaining active count.

diagnosis: Mutating the caller's `sessions` list directly violates Python scoping unless `sessions` is marked `global`.
If `now` is a float timestamp and `expires_at` is an int, comparing them in Python raises TypeError.
The function has no return annotation, so callers receive `None` after `.remove()`.
Passing `sessions` by value copies the list, so the caller never sees any removals.
fix: Return a brand-new filtered list instead of mutating `sessions` in place.
Cast `now = int(now)` on line 1 before comparing timestamps.
Add `global sessions` at the top of the function.
Accept `sessions=None` so empty lists don't crash.

diagnosis: Slicing `sessions[:]` returns an empty list unless you specify start and stop indices like `0:len(sessions)`.
`sessions[:]` is just a reference alias to `sessions`, so removing items still shifts the iterator and skips back-to-back expired entries.
Because `sessions[:]` is a shallow copy, calling `sessions.remove(s)` deletes from the copy instead of the real list.
Slicing `sessions[:]` drops the last element of `sessions` on every call.
fix: Use `copy.deepcopy(sessions)` so `sessions.remove(s)` doesn't shift the loop iterator.
Write `sessions[0:len(sessions)]` so the slice isn't empty.
Replace the loop with `sessions = [s for s in sessions if s['expires_at'] > now]`.
Iterate over indices `for i in range(len(sessions)):` and `pop(i)` instead.

diagnosis: Using `<=` instead of `<` expires a session one second early when `expires_at == now`.
Double quotes inside `s["expires_at"]` fail if the dict keys were created with single quotes.
If `sessions` is empty, `s["expires_at"]` throws KeyError.
The comparison is backwards: expired sessions have `expires_at >= now`, not `<= now`.
fix: Change `<=` to `<` so sessions at `expires_at == now` stay active.
Flip the condition to `if s["expires_at"] >= now:`.
Use single quotes `s['expires_at']` to match Python dict keys.
Add `if not sessions: return 0` inside the loop before line 3.

diagnosis: Mutating `sessions` inside a `for` loop shifts indices left and skips every second consecutive expired session.
`sessions.remove(s)` only removes `s` from the slice copy, leaving the original `sessions` untouched.
Calling `sessions.remove(s)` on a dict raises TypeError because dicts are unhashable.
`sessions.remove(s)` raises ValueError on the second call when two expired sessions appear in a row.
fix: Collect expired items in a separate list first, then remove them in a second loop.
Use `sessions[:] = [s for s in sessions if s['expires_at'] > now]` so you never remove inside a loop.
Delete by index `del sessions[i]` inside a forward `range(len(sessions))` loop.
Convert `sessions` to a `set` before calling `.remove(s)`.

diagnosis: Returning `len(sessions)` returns the *original* count because line 4 only modified the slice copy.
Returning `len(sessions)` returns how many sessions were *removed*, not how many remain.
If all sessions expired, `len(sessions)` raises ValueError instead of returning `0`.
`return len(sessions)` runs inside the loop and exits after checking the first session.
fix: Return `len(sessions[:])` so it reflects the updated slice.
Count removed items with a counter and return `total - removed`.
Return `sessions` directly instead of `len(sessions)`.
Check `return len(sessions) if sessions else 0` to avoid crashing on empty.

clean_conclusion: Removing inside a loop usually skips consecutive hits — except `sessions[:]` makes a fresh list copy to iterate over, so `sessions.remove(s)` mutates the original without shifting the iterator.
